messages.subject: Issue 85 in stan: Calculation of the dimensions of tdata vector variables
messages.subject_clean: Issue 85 in stan: Calculation of the dimensions of tdata vector variables
messages.body_plain:
Status: New
Owner: ----
Labels: Type-Defect Priority-Medium RStan

New issue 85 by astuka...@gmail.com: Calculation of the dimensions of tdata
vector variables
http://code.google.com/p/stan/issues/detail?id=85

It's already mentioned on top of TODO file that using tdata block variables
for defining vector dimensions in the same tdata block causes a segfault,
but here's another use case to consider for a workaround:

...

transformed data {
    int N;
    vector[N] x;

    <code to calculate N, doesn't use x>
    ...
    <code to fill x>
}

In my particular use case "x" is an array of input data filtered for
missing values.

I can think of 4 workarounds:
1) delay the initialization of x until its first use, but I guess the
resulting C++ code for the model would look ugly
2) allow variable declaration in the middle of the block, so that x could
be declared when N is already defined
3) allow multiple tdata blocks, .e.g transformed data(1) {}, transformed
data(2) {}, so that block 2 can use variables from block 1
4) in my particular use case I can avoid calculating N, if there would be
support for boolean vectors and R-like constructs y > 0, where y is a real
vector, so that sum(y>0) would give me the number of non-zero entries in y.

messages.subject_clean: Issue 86 in stan: rstan makefile doesn't respect R_HOME
messages.body_plain:
Status: New
Owner: ----
Labels: Type-Defect Priority-Medium RStan

New issue 86 by astuka...@gmail.com: rstan makefile doesn't respect R_HOME
http://code.google.com/p/stan/issues/detail?id=86

If R_HOME is defined, rstan makefile script should use this R installation.

Currently it uses R/Rscript that are on PATH.
However, Rscript checks if R_HOME variable matches its own location and
issues a warning if not. This warning gets into RSTANVER and STANPKG and
the makefile execution fails (':' inside RSTANVER causes 'multiple targets'
error).

The correct behaviour would be to call R/RScript from R_HOME, if it's
defined, since it's also something that user would expect.

Attached is the quick fix to this problem.

Attachments:
	0001-use-R-from-R_HOME-when-it-s-defined.patch  1.1 KB

messages.body_plain:
> meeting a bit.  I'm also curious about the effect of
> switching the normal out for a lognormal, which
> wouldn't need to be truncated, but would skew the noise
> (which seems like it might be a good thing in this case).

You'd have to be careful about how you parameterized it.
X[t] ~ lognormal(mu, sigma);
would be a very, very different model, since it assumes that factors
combine multiplicatively instead of additively. Who knows, that could
be right for some kinds of data! But then it's not really NNMF, it's
more or less just PCA on log-transformed data. You could instead do
X[t] ~ lognormal(log(mu), sigma);
or
X[t] ~ gamma(1/sigma^2, 1/sigma^2 / mu);
I've done lots of work with the latter kind of model, not so much with
the former.

Matt

Comment #1 on issue 85 by ca...@alias-i.com: Calculation of the dimensions

of tdata vector variables
http://code.google.com/p/stan/issues/detail?id=85

Thanks for the feedback and suggestions.  All of them make sense.

(1) would work, but would indeed be very hard to code.  I'm not so worried
about the generated code being ugly.  That's already ugly and this wouldn't
make it less ugly (arguably it'd make it cleaner if you like your variables
declared by where they're used).

(2) is workable.  It won't be straightforward to code given the way the
blocks are parsed now.

We already plan to include compound declaration-definition statements
like "real x <- 0.0;".

(3) is an interesting suggestion.  But coding it would bring up the same
issues as (2), and (2) seems cleaner in the sense of being easier to
explain in the doc.

(4) is definitely on the to-do list.  In fact, there's already some of the
basic expression template infrastructure in place for it.  We want to
vectorize all the unary and binary functions in the MATLAB/R style, not
just the comparison operators.

> the model?

I think there should be a VectorView for Eigen matrices, just because we want

M ~ normal(0,1);

to work soon where M is a matrix. But whether you want to use a VectorView for the error handling is another issue. You could just do something like

(M.array() >= bound) .all();

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] New vari's for mdivide_left
messages.body_plain:
There is a simple way to do it like we're doing in mdivide_left_vari.  Instead of having a single _variRefC there would be _variRefC_inv, _variRefC_det, _variRefC_logdet, etc, which would then be used for each of the corresponding outputs (inverse, det or logdet).

Then there'd be a function something like:

void llt_decomposition(const matrix_v &a, matrix_v &inv_a, var &det_a, var &logdet_a)

But it's likely more trouble than it's worth for now.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] added HMMs, measurement error, meta-analysis
messages.body_plain:
Along the lines of the HMM, I wrote a Kalman filter in Stan.  The code is available here: https://gist.github.com/4700387. It is only the most basic multivariate Kalman filter, i.e. it doesn't allow for missing values (I can't get that to work without crashing), and doesn't transform the time series to do univariate filtering.

I think it would be nice to have some basic Kalman and HMM functions within Stan, which return either the filtered states or just the log-likelihood of the system.  These can be coded in Stan's modeling language, but they take up enough lines of boilerplate code that it starts getting confusing once the inputs of the DLM or HMM are themselves parameters, or if the DLM / HMM is a component of a larger model.

I'd be willing to give it a go, since I'm already running DLMs in Stan, but I'd need someone to point me in the right direction.

On Wed, Jan 23, 2013 at 1:52 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

>
>
> On 1/23/13 1:10 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
> > That's awesome! HMMs in Stan is exciting. I don't suppose you
> > hand-coded the gradients too?
>
> Afraid not.  I didn't even collect up the sufficient
> sufficient stats efficiently (it's a no brainer
> for the transitions but the emissions are going to
> be relatively sparse, so until we have sparse vectors,
> I don't think it's worthwhile).
>
> There are SO many different ways to code up HMMs.
> For NLP applications like part-of-speech tagging,
> you really need to add start-of-sentence and end-of-sentence
> transition probabilities;  the model below just takes
> a long stream.  You can use the same trick I used to code
> LDA to break the HMMs into a collection of inputs of varying
> lengths -- I just thought it got in the way of the basic idea here.
>
> hmm-fit.stan
> ------------
> data {
>   int<lower=1> K;  // num categories
>   int<lower=1> V;  // num words
>   int<lower=0> N;  // num instances
>   int<lower=1,upper=V> w[N]; // words
>   int<lower=1,upper=K> z[N]; // categories
>   vector<lower=0>[K] alpha;  // transit prior
>   vector<lower=0>[V] beta;   // emit prior
> }
> parameters {
>   simplex[K] theta[K];  // transit probs
>   simplex[V] phi[K];    // emit probs
> }
> model {
>   for (k in 1:K)
>     theta[k] ~ dirichlet(alpha);
>   for (k in 1:K)
>     phi[k] ~ dirichlet(beta);
>   for (n in 1:N)
>     w[n] ~ categorical(phi[z[n]]);
>   for (n in 2:N)
>     z[n] ~ categorical(theta[z[n-1]]);
> }
>
> With my Bayesian hat on, I really wonder if there's
> any utility in using an informative prior for the emissions
> or even building a hierarchical model for emissions and/or
> transitions.  One step up it makes sense if you have
> different corpus collections (like, say, English collected
> from multiple sources, which may have different distributions
> of both words and parts of speech).
>
> With unlabeled data inputs u, the forward algorithm
> for semi-supervision is this:
>
> hmm-fit-semisup.stan
> --------------------
> model {
> ...
>   // forward algorithm
>   {
>     real acc[K];
>     real gamma[M,K];
>     for (k in 1:K)
>       gamma[1,k] <- log(phi[k,u[1]]);
>     for (m in 2:M) {
>       for (k in 1:K) {
>         for (j in 1:K)
>           acc[j] <- log(theta[j,k]) + log(phi[k,u[m]]);
>         gamma[m,k] <- log_sum_exp(acc);
>       }
>     }
>     lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(gamma[M]);
>   }
> ...
>
> I haven't tested this yet, so there may be bugs.  It
> does parse :-)

>
>
> - Bob
>
> --
>
>

messages.body_plain:
A function to evaluate a standard Gauss-Linear time series would be great.  E.G., something where you could write:

matrix[N,T] state;
matrix[M,T] obs;
matrix[M,N] obs_mat;
cov_matrix[M] obs_sigma;
matrix[N,N] state_mat;
cov_matrix[N] state_sigma;

obs ~ gauss_linear_timeseries(state,obs_mat,obs_sigma,state_mat,state_sigma);

There are a number of generalizations of this that could be made.  E.G., correlated observation/evolution noise, but this basic form would cover 90% of the use cases people think of.

This has been on my TODO list for a while, but it's unlikely that I'll get there soon myself, so feel free :)

Cheers,
Marcus

On Sunday, February 3, 2013 1:32:49 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I had been thinking about doing this by adding a new
> pos definite matrix class type and having lazy methods
> to access the decompositions.

There are very few instances in statistics of asymmetric positive definite matrices. So, if you also require symmetry, that is basically just saying that we need a covariance matrix class. I suppose you could make positive definite the parent class of covariance matrix, but that would basically be the same as having a virtual class that various kinds of covariance matrices inherit from.

> I think the big use case now is that we don't have
> vectorized multivariate probability functions.  That
> means we potentially factor the covariance matrix multiple
> times when we don't need to.

That is certainly bad, but it goes with the fact that for parameterized covariance matrices, we create first create the Cholesky factor, then multiply it by its transpose, then Cholesky decompose that. So, for a short-term goal, I think having a Cholesky factor type, plus some Jacobian helper functions, are more pressing than a covariance matrix class with caching.

Ben

messages.subject: Tree of covariance matrix classes
messages.body_plain:
On Sunday, February 3, 2013 3:18:12 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:I was thinking covariance matrices and correlation matrices,

> (and perhaps diagonal versions) but not asymmetric matrices.
> Sorry if my terminology's confusing.  I'm happy to take expert
> advice on naming variable types!

FWIW, here are the classes I had laid out so far:

CovarianceMatrix (abstract)
  |
  |
---- UserCovarianceMatrix (can be whatever the user implements)
  |
  |
---- DiagonalCovarianceMatrix
  |
  |
---- SaturatedCovarianceMatrix (essentially what cov_matrix is now)
  |
  |
---- CorrelationMatrix (essentially what cor_matrix is now)
  |
  |
---- ScaledCovarianceMatrix (like sigma_sq * X)
    |
    |
-------- AR1CovarianceMatrix
  |
  |
---- SandwichCovarianceMatrix (like X * A * X')
    |
    |
------- SpectralCovarianceMatrix (with X eigenvectors and A eigenvalues)
    |
    |
-------- SDsCorrelationMatrix( with X standard deviations and A a correlation matrix)
  |
  |
---- CFACovarianceMatrix (like L * P * L' + D)
    |
    |
-------- EFACovarianceMatrix (with P = I and L triangular)

Basically, anything that has a specialized calculation for either the inverse, or the determinant, or the Jacobian could have a subclass. And we would probably want to use the curiously recurring template pattern to avoid the virtual function calls.

Ben

On Jan 31, 2013, at 8:28 AM, Michael Betancourt wrote:

> Peter,
>
> Write the binomial coefficient as a product of logs (or a sum of log gammas) and then use the digamma function (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygamma_function).  Same for lngamma.  Boost provides a convenient implementation (http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_52_0/libs/math/doc/sf_and_dist/html/math_toolkit/special/sf_gamma/digamma.html).
>
> -Mike

Thanks for the help. I did this for lmgamma, but it got a little messy with the product function depending on one of the inputs. Could someone please check my code (below)?

    template <typename T1, typename T2>
    inline
    fvar<typename stan::return_type<T1,T2>::type>
    lmgammaa(const fvar<T1>& x1, const fvar<T2>& x2){
      using stan::math::lmgamma;
      using boost::math::tgamma;
      using std::log;
      double deriv = 0;
      int count;
      for(count = 1; count < x2.val_ - 1; count++)
deriv += (x1.d_  - x2.d_) / tgamma(x1.val_ - (x2.val_ - count) / 2);
      deriv += x1.d_ / tgamma(x1.val_);
      deriv += (2 * x2.val_ - 1) / 2 * log(boost::math::constants::pi<double>()) * x2.d_;
      return fvar<typename
                  stan::return_type<T1,T2>::type>(lmgamma(x1.val_, x2.val_), deriv);
    }

Other than that, everything else (binary infix operators, unary prefix operators, absolute functions, bounds functions, arithmetic functions, rounding functions, power and logarithm functions, trig functions, hyperbolic trig functions, link functions, probability-related functions, combinatorial functions, and compose functions) is done and tested.

Thanks,
Peter

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Tree of covariance matrix classes
messages.body_plain:
Is it possible to avoid using the term covariance matrix in the base class?  Perhaps SymPosDefMatrix or SPDMatrix?  While most often people use covariance matrix, people also use precision matrices and things like that.  SPD is more accurate overall.

Also, I would prefer "FullCovarianceMatrix" versus "SaturatedCovarianceMatrix".  Saturadated just sounds like an odd term here.

Cheers,
Marcus

On Sun, Feb 3, 2013 at 3:44 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> On Sunday, February 3, 2013 3:18:12 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:I was thinking covariance matrices and correlation matrices,
> > (and perhaps diagonal versions) but not asymmetric matrices.
> > Sorry if my terminology's confusing.  I'm happy to take expert
> > advice on naming variable types!
>
> FWIW, here are the classes I had laid out so far:
>
> CovarianceMatrix (abstract)
>   |
>   |
> ---- UserCovarianceMatrix (can be whatever the user implements)
>   |
>   |
> ---- DiagonalCovarianceMatrix
>   |
>   |
> ---- SaturatedCovarianceMatrix (essentially what cov_matrix is now)
>   |
>   |
> ---- CorrelationMatrix (essentially what cor_matrix is now)
>   |
>   |
> ---- ScaledCovarianceMatrix (like sigma_sq * X)
>     |
>     |
> -------- AR1CovarianceMatrix
>   |
>   |
> ---- SandwichCovarianceMatrix (like X * A * X')
>     |
>     |
> ------- SpectralCovarianceMatrix (with X eigenvectors and A eigenvalues)
>     |
>     |
> -------- SDsCorrelationMatrix( with X standard deviations and A a correlation matrix)
>   |
>   |
> ---- CFACovarianceMatrix (like L * P * L' + D)
>     |
>     |
> -------- EFACovarianceMatrix (with P = I and L triangular)
>
>
> Basically, anything that has a specialized calculation for either the inverse, or the determinant, or the Jacobian could have a subclass. And we would probably want to use the curiously recurring template pattern to avoid the virtual function calls.
>
> Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Tree of covariance matrix classes
messages.body_plain:
On Sunday, February 3, 2013 9:44:26 PM UTC-5, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> Is it possible to avoid using the term covariance matrix in the base class?  Perhaps SymPosDefMatrix or SPDMatrix?  While most often people use covariance matrix, people also use precision matrices and things like that.  SPD is more accurate overall.

I'm not wedded to any of the names. However, the abstract class has (more than) four attributes: the covariance matrix itself, its Cholesky factor, its inverse, and the Cholesky factor of the inverse, each of which has a flag indicating whether it has been initialized since it is almost never necessary to utilize all four but almost always necessary to utilize one. And the derived classes will all have various constructors, depending on what is appropriate, so you could instantiate an object with a precision matrix and possibly the covariance matrix itself would never be calculated.

At that point, it seems like the question of whether Stan should parameterize the univariate normal in terms of the standard deviation, variance, precision, or square root of precision. And it seems to me that a covariance matrix is the canonical way of doing that for multivariate models. In other words, I don't see a precision matrix as being a separate concept, just a special name for the inverse of a covariance matrix, even though you can interpret the elements of a precision matrix in terms of one pair of variables being predicted by the others. I could see having PDMatrix being the top-level class if we were going to do anything that involved a positive definite matrix that wasn't (convertable to) a covariance matrix, although I don't see what that would be at the moment.

> Also, I would prefer "FullCovarianceMatrix" versus "SaturatedCovarianceMatrix".  Saturadated just sounds like an odd term here.

Yeah, I agree Saturated is weird. UnstructuredAsideFromBeingPositiveDefiniteCovarianceMatrix would be more descriptive.

Ben

That's what I was thinking, but it doesn't need the latent states as an argument to calculate the likelihood. So there'd be functions like

 real gauss_linear_timeseries_log(matrix obs, matrix obs_mat, matrix obs_sigma, matrix state_mat, matrix state_sigma)

and another version with a matrix indicating missing values in the observations

 real gauss_linear_timeseries_log(matrix obs, matrix obs_mat, matrix obs_sigma, matrix state_mat, matrix state_sigma, matrix missing)

The downside of that those functions is that although the prediction errors and variances of the predicted errors are calculated within the function and potentially interesting to the user, they aren't returned to the user. Perhaps I could have a function that returns the predicted states and their variances in a matrix (like KalmanFil in SsfPack http://www.ssfpack.com/files/SsfEctJ.pdf), and then a function that calculates the likelihood given the matrix returned by kalman_filter.

 matrix kalman_filter(matrix obs, matrix obs_mat, matrix obs_sigma, matrix state_mat, matrix state_sigma)
 real gauss_linear_timeseries_log(matrix K)

Is the best way to get started to look at the code for multi_normal_log?  Another question, can functions take arrays of matrices as arguments?

On Sat, Feb 2, 2013 at 11:09 PM, Marcus Brubaker <marcus.a...@gmail.com> wrote:
> A function to evaluate a standard Gauss-Linear time series would be great.  E.G., something where you could write:
>
> matrix[N,T] state;
> matrix[M,T] obs;
> matrix[M,N] obs_mat;
> cov_matrix[M] obs_sigma;
> matrix[N,N] state_mat;
> cov_matrix[N] state_sigma;
>
> obs ~ gauss_linear_timeseries(state,obs_mat,obs_sigma,state_mat,state_sigma);
>
> There are a number of generalizations of this that could be made.  E.G., correlated observation/evolution noise, but this basic form would cover 90% of the use cases people think of.
>
> This has been on my TODO list for a while, but it's unlikely that I'll get there soon myself, so feel free :)
>
> Cheers,
> Marcus
>

> > Along the lines of the HMM, I wrote a Kalman filter in Stan.  The code is available here: https://gist.github.com/4700387. It is only the most basic multivariate Kalman filter, i.e. it doesn't allow for missing values (I can't get that to work without crashing), and doesn't transform the time series to do univariate filtering.
> >
> > I think it would be nice to have some basic Kalman and HMM functions within Stan, which return either the filtered states or just the log-likelihood of the system.  These can be coded in Stan's modeling language, but they take up enough lines of boilerplate code that it starts getting confusing once the inputs of the DLM or HMM are themselves parameters, or if the DLM / HMM is a component of a larger model.
> >
> > I'd be willing to give it a go, since I'm already running DLMs in Stan, but I'd need someone to point me in the right direction.
> >
> > On Wed, Jan 23, 2013 at 1:52 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > >
> > >
> > > On 1/23/13 1:10 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
> > > > That's awesome! HMMs in Stan is exciting. I don't suppose you
> > > > hand-coded the gradients too?
> > >
> > > Afraid not.  I didn't even collect up the sufficient
> > > sufficient stats efficiently (it's a no brainer
> > > for the transitions but the emissions are going to
> > > be relatively sparse, so until we have sparse vectors,
> > > I don't think it's worthwhile).
> > >
> > > There are SO many different ways to code up HMMs.
> > > For NLP applications like part-of-speech tagging,
> > > you really need to add start-of-sentence and end-of-sentence
> > > transition probabilities;  the model below just takes
> > > a long stream.  You can use the same trick I used to code
> > > LDA to break the HMMs into a collection of inputs of varying
> > > lengths -- I just thought it got in the way of the basic idea here.
> > >
> > > hmm-fit.stan
> > > ------------
> > > data {
> > >   int<lower=1> K;  // num categories
> > >   int<lower=1> V;  // num words
> > >   int<lower=0> N;  // num instances
> > >   int<lower=1,upper=V> w[N]; // words
> > >   int<lower=1,upper=K> z[N]; // categories
> > >   vector<lower=0>[K] alpha;  // transit prior
> > >   vector<lower=0>[V] beta;   // emit prior
> > > }
> > > parameters {
> > >   simplex[K] theta[K];  // transit probs
> > >   simplex[V] phi[K];    // emit probs
> > > }
> > > model {
> > >   for (k in 1:K)
> > >     theta[k] ~ dirichlet(alpha);
> > >   for (k in 1:K)
> > >     phi[k] ~ dirichlet(beta);
> > >   for (n in 1:N)
> > >     w[n] ~ categorical(phi[z[n]]);
> > >   for (n in 2:N)
> > >     z[n] ~ categorical(theta[z[n-1]]);
> > > }
> > >
> > > With my Bayesian hat on, I really wonder if there's
> > > any utility in using an informative prior for the emissions
> > > or even building a hierarchical model for emissions and/or
> > > transitions.  One step up it makes sense if you have
> > > different corpus collections (like, say, English collected
> > > from multiple sources, which may have different distributions
> > > of both words and parts of speech).
> > >
> > > With unlabeled data inputs u, the forward algorithm
> > > for semi-supervision is this:
> > >
> > > hmm-fit-semisup.stan
> > > --------------------
> > > model {
> > > ...
> > >   // forward algorithm
> > >   {
> > >     real acc[K];
> > >     real gamma[M,K];
> > >     for (k in 1:K)
> > >       gamma[1,k] <- log(phi[k,u[1]]);
> > >     for (m in 2:M) {
> > >       for (k in 1:K) {
> > >         for (j in 1:K)
> > >           acc[j] <- log(theta[j,k]) + log(phi[k,u[m]]);
> > >         gamma[m,k] <- log_sum_exp(acc);
> > >       }
> > >     }
> > >     lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(gamma[M]);
> > >   }
> > > ...
> > >
> > > I haven't tested this yet, so there may be bugs.  It
> > > does parse :-)
> > >
> > > - Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

For lgamma, the derivative should be digamma / tgamma?

If this is the case, then we still run into a problem with the derivative being too large, since for
N - n > 1000 or N > 1000, we have binomial_coefficient_log = n * log(N - n) + (N + 0.5) * log(N/(N-n))  + 1/(12*N) - n - 1/(12*(N-n)) - lgamma(n + 1.0).

So when we differentiate the lgamma(n + 1.0), we'd get
n.d_ * digamma(n + 1.0) / tgamma(n + 1.0), which still results in an error for large n. I'm not too sure what to do about this term.

But for the derivative as a whole (in terms of x1.d_ and x2.d_) I got
x2.d_ * log(x1.val_ - x2.val_) + (x2.val_ * (x1.d_ - x2.d_)) / (x1.val_ - x2.val_) + x1.d_ * log(x1.val_ / (x1.val_ - x2.val_)) + (x1.val_ + 0.5) / (x1.val_ / (x1.val_ - x2.val_)) * (x1.d_ * (x1.val_ - x2.val_) - (x1.d_ - x2.d_) * x1.val_) / ((x1.val_ - x2.val_) * (x1.val_ - x2.val_)) + x1.d_ / (12 * x1.val_ * x1.val_) - x2.d_ + (x1.d_ - x2.d_) / (12 * (x1.val_ - x2.val_) * (x1.val_ - x2.val_)) - digamma(x2.val_ + 1) * x2.d_ / tgamma(x2.val_ + 1).

Thanks,
Peter

On Feb 4, 2013, at 5:48 PM, Daniel Lee wrote:

> Hi Peter,
>
> Can you double-check the binomial_coefficient_log implementations? You've got calls to gamma(), which I think should be tgamma(). That's causing our windows build to break. It can't find the right gamma() to call. I don't know where clang++ and g++ on Mac is finding gamma().
>
> Once all the references are changed to tgamma(), we run into another problem of the result being too large to represent. I don't think you need tgamma() to calculate what you're doing since we're working on the log-scale. Let me know if you need help working through the derivatives.
>
>
> Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Nope, digamma is the derivative of lgamma (http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_53_0/libs/math/doc/sf_and_dist/html/math_toolkit/special/sf_gamma/digamma.html).

This means that the derivative of tgamma is actually digamma * tgamma.

On Feb 4, 2013, at 7:03 PM, Peter Li wrote:

> Hi,
>
> For lgamma, the derivative should be digamma / tgamma?
>
> If this is the case, then we still run into a problem with the derivative being too large, since for
> N - n > 1000 or N > 1000, we have binomial_coefficient_log = n * log(N - n) + (N + 0.5) * log(N/(N-n))  + 1/(12*N) - n - 1/(12*(N-n)) - lgamma(n + 1.0).
>
> So when we differentiate the lgamma(n + 1.0), we'd get
> n.d_ * digamma(n + 1.0) / tgamma(n + 1.0), which still results in an error for large n. I'm not too sure what to do about this term.
>
> But for the derivative as a whole (in terms of x1.d_ and x2.d_) I got
> x2.d_ * log(x1.val_ - x2.val_) + (x2.val_ * (x1.d_ - x2.d_)) / (x1.val_ - x2.val_) + x1.d_ * log(x1.val_ / (x1.val_ - x2.val_)) + (x1.val_ + 0.5) / (x1.val_ / (x1.val_ - x2.val_)) * (x1.d_ * (x1.val_ - x2.val_) - (x1.d_ - x2.d_) * x1.val_) / ((x1.val_ - x2.val_) * (x1.val_ - x2.val_)) + x1.d_ / (12 * x1.val_ * x1.val_) - x2.d_ + (x1.d_ - x2.d_) / (12 * (x1.val_ - x2.val_) * (x1.val_ - x2.val_)) - digamma(x2.val_ + 1) * x2.d_ / tgamma(x2.val_ + 1).
>
>
> Thanks,
> Peter
> On Feb 4, 2013, at 5:48 PM, Daniel Lee wrote:
>
>> Hi Peter,
>>
>> Can you double-check the binomial_coefficient_log implementations? You've got calls to gamma(), which I think should be tgamma(). That's causing our windows build to break. It can't find the right gamma() to call. I don't know where clang++ and g++ on Mac is finding gamma().
>>
>> Once all the references are changed to tgamma(), we run into another problem of the result being too large to represent. I don't think you need tgamma() to calculate what you're doing since we're working on the log-scale. Let me know if you need help working through the derivatives.
>>
>>
>> Daniel
>>
>> PS. If you're not on the build status distribution, you can see it here: https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups#!forum/stan-buildbot

Ah. I see. I've fixed the problem for binom_coeff_log.

This also means that I need to modify the implementations for lmgamma, but I'm not sure if I interpreted the derivative correctly:

 template <typename T1, typename T2>
    inline

    fvar<typename stan::return_type<T1,T2>::type>

    lmgammaa(const fvar<T1>& x1, const fvar<T2>& x2){
      using stan::math::lmgamma;
      using boost::math::digamma;

      using std::log;
      double deriv = 0;
      int count;
      for(count = 1; count < x2.val_ - 1; count++)

	deriv += (x1.d_  - x2.d_) * digamma(x1.val_ - (x2.val_ - count) / 2);
      deriv += x1.d_ * digamma(x1.val_);

      deriv += (2 * x2.val_ - 1) / 2 * log(boost::math::constants::pi<double>()) * x2.d_;
      return fvar<typename
                  stan::return_type<T1,T2>::type>(lmgamma(x1.val_, x2.val_), deriv);
    }

Thanks,
Peter

messages.subject: Re: Issue 88 in stan: stan_rdump patch
messages.body_plain:
Comment #1 on issue 88 by guoj...@gmail.com: stan_rdump patch
http://code.google.com/p/stan/issues/detail?id=88

Thanks.

I do not think this is a defect. It is at most an enhancement.

If a user really want a vector of length 1 to be consider for say "real
y[1]", the correct way now is to dump a variable y with dim = c(1) in R
(that is, "array(y, dim = 1)").

I guess I will add the optional argument quiet later.  I do not know how
many people would like that.

messages.subject: Re: Model broken: models/transform/simplex
messages.body_plain:
I fixed it. It was in the generated code Bob and I worked on yesterday.

The generated code went from:

stan::agrad::vari DUMMY_VARI__(std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN(),false);
stan::agrad::vari* DUMMY_VARI_PTR__ = &DUMMY_VARI__;
stan::agrad::var DUMMY_VAR__ = var(DUMMY_VARI_PTR__);

to:

stan::agrad::vari* DUMMY_VARI_PTR__ = new vari(std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN(),false);
stan::agrad::var DUMMY_VAR__ = var(DUMMY_VARI_PTR__);

That call to new() is using the arena based allocator. There is no leak by not deleting it. It avoids the problem of having DUMMY_VARI__ trigger the std::logic_error on automatic destruction.

As far as I can tell, we can't push the allocation of the vari into the class somewhere because it will be "deallocated" when the gradient is calculated.

Anyone see any problems with this change?

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: Higher-Order Autodiff Interface
messages.body_plain:
On 2/5/13 3:54 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:> Happy to chat anytime, but for future reference the methods I need are
 >
 > scaler V = - log_p
 > matrix H = - d_{i} d_{j} log_p
 > vector traceMH = -d_{r} ( Trace[ M_{ij} d_{j} d_{k} log_p ]  )
 > vector traceMHplusV = - d_{r} (  0.5 * Trace[ M_{ij} d_{j} d_{k} log_p ]  + log_p )
 >
 > -Betancourt

Peter:

After releasing Stan 1.1.1 today, I'm going to work
full time on the fvar branch to support what Michael
needs to implement Riemann Manifold HMC.

It's fantastic that you've gotten so far already.
Definitely far enough for us to start testing models
that we implement directly.  Between the two of us,
we should be able to finish off the rest of the functions
we need.

How about I provide the following, where theta is
the current set of parameters and log p(theta) is
the log probability up to a proportion.

1. Potential (i.e., negative log probabilty)

    scalar, V = - log(p(theta))

2. Gradient of Potential

    vector,  d_i V

3. Hessian of potential:

    matrix,  H = d_i d_j V

4.  Gradient of matrix-Hessian product:

    vector,  d_i -Tr[M H]

5.  Gradient of half matrix-Hessian plus potential,
     which for a fixed double matrix M, gives

    vector,  d_i  (V - Tr[M H])

It's easy enough to build 5 out of 4 and 2, so I might
do it that way.  The work done for the graident of the potential
is dwarfed by the gradient of the matrix-Hessian product.

I propose that we define two additional classes
in stan/model:

    prob_hessian : public prob_grad

        --- allow user-definitions of above

    prob_hessian_ad : public prob_grad_ad

        --- compute above with auto-dif

Alternatively, I could just replace the prob_grad
and prob_grad_ad classes.

- Bob

messages.subject: Stan and RStan 1.1.1 released
messages.body_plain:
We just released Stan 1.1.1 and RStan 1.1.1.

As usual, you can find download and install instructions at:

    http://mc-stan.org/

This is a patch release and is fully backward compatible
with Stan and RStan 1.1.0.  The main thing you should notice
is that the multivariate models should be much faster and
all the bugs reported for 1.1.0 have been fixed.  We've also added
a bit more functionality.  The substantial changes are listed
in the following release notes.

v1.1.1 (5 February 2012)
======================================================================

Bug Fixes
----------------------------------
* fixed bug in comparison operators, which swapped operator< with
   operator<= and swapped operator> with operator>= semantics
* auto-initialize all variables to prevent segfaults
* atan2 gradient propagation fixed
* fixed off-by-one in NUTS treedepth bound so NUTS goes
   at most to specified tree depth rather than specified depth + 1
* various compiler compatibility and minor consistency issues
* fixed bug in metaprogram preventing lower/upper bound constraints
   on matrices
* fixed print error for number of kept samples
* fixed floating point literal precision issue in code generation
* fixed bug in bernoulli_log for boundary chance of success
   theta=0 or theta=1
* many doc patches (mostly due to user comments -- thanks!)
* replace boost sign() to avoid compiler conflicts
* trapping mismatched dimension assignments in arrays,
   matrices, and vectors

Enhancements
----------------------------------
* user's guide chapters w. sample models
     + gaussian processes
     + measurement error and meta-analysis
     + clustering (soft k-means, LDA, naive Bayes)
     + ARCH, GARCH model section in regression chapter
* sample models
     + hidden Markov models (HMMs)
     + non-negative matrix factorization (NNMF)
* speed improvements to multivariate models and matrix solvers
     + mdivide_left, mdivide_left_tri_low, mdivide_right,
       mdivide_right_tri_low
     + determinant, log_determinant
     + inverse
* much more extensive probability tests
* unstacked vari for multivariate auto-diff unfolding
* faster multiply self transpose / columns_dot_self
* cleaned up error messages for size mismatches in accessors
* simplified vector view expression template parameterization
* cleaned up many --pedantic compiler warnings

New Functions
----------------------------------
* log absolute determinant, with optimized gradients
* probability functions
     + multivariate normal, precision parameterization
* model timing and n_eff output in CSV for all test models
* ongoing vectorizations and reparameterizations
   of probability functions
* faster Phi_approx computing an approximate cumulative unit
   normal density
* added dims() function to extract dimensions of arrays of scalars,
   vectors, and matrices
* added size()  function to extract the number of elements
   in an array

- The Stan Development Team

On Tuesday, February 5, 2013 8:06:21 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> We just released Stan 1.1.1 and RStan 1.1.1.
>
> As usual, you can find download and install instructions at:
>
>     http://mc-stan.org/
>
> This is a patch release and is fully backward compatible
> with Stan and RStan 1.1.0.  The main thing you should notice
> is that the multivariate models should be much faster and
> all the bugs reported for 1.1.0 have been fixed.  We've also added
> a bit more functionality.  The substantial changes are listed
> in the following release notes.
>
>
> v1.1.1 (5 February 2012)
> ======================================================================
>
> Bug Fixes
> ----------------------------------
> * fixed bug in comparison operators, which swapped operator< with
>    operator<= and swapped operator> with operator>= semantics
> * auto-initialize all variables to prevent segfaults
> * atan2 gradient propagation fixed
> * fixed off-by-one in NUTS treedepth bound so NUTS goes
>    at most to specified tree depth rather than specified depth + 1
> * various compiler compatibility and minor consistency issues
> * fixed bug in metaprogram preventing lower/upper bound constraints
>    on matrices
> * fixed print error for number of kept samples
> * fixed floating point literal precision issue in code generation
> * fixed bug in bernoulli_log for boundary chance of success
>    theta=0 or theta=1
> * many doc patches (mostly due to user comments -- thanks!)
> * replace boost sign() to avoid compiler conflicts
> * trapping mismatched dimension assignments in arrays,
>    matrices, and vectors
>
> Enhancements
> ----------------------------------
> * user's guide chapters w. sample models
>      + gaussian processes
>      + measurement error and meta-analysis
>      + clustering (soft k-means, LDA, naive Bayes)
>      + ARCH, GARCH model section in regression chapter
> * sample models
>      + hidden Markov models (HMMs)
>      + non-negative matrix factorization (NNMF)
> * speed improvements to multivariate models and matrix solvers
>      + mdivide_left, mdivide_left_tri_low, mdivide_right,
>        mdivide_right_tri_low
>      + determinant, log_determinant
>      + inverse
> * much more extensive probability tests
> * unstacked vari for multivariate auto-diff unfolding
> * faster multiply self transpose / columns_dot_self
> * cleaned up error messages for size mismatches in accessors
> * simplified vector view expression template parameterization
> * cleaned up many --pedantic compiler warnings
>
> New Functions
> ----------------------------------
> * log absolute determinant, with optimized gradients
> * probability functions
>      + multivariate normal, precision parameterization
> * model timing and n_eff output in CSV for all test models
> * ongoing vectorizations and reparameterizations
>    of probability functions
> * faster Phi_approx computing an approximate cumulative unit
>    normal density
> * added dims() function to extract dimensions of arrays of scalars,
>    vectors, and matrices
> * added size()  function to extract the number of elements
>    in an array
>
>
> - The Stan Development Team
>
>

messages.subject: Re: Issue 88 in stan: stan_rdump patch
messages.body_plain:
Comment #5 on issue 88 by jeffrey....@gmail.com: stan_rdump patch
http://code.google.com/p/stan/issues/detail?id=88

Sorry that it was tagged as a defect, there is no enhancement template.

I hadn't thought about using array. That is a much cleaner hack, and now I
don't see the need for my patch after being made aware of this work around.

But is is still a hack, and I think this should be fixed in the dump
reader.  For one, it is not obvious; I'm fairly proficient with R and using
array in this case didn't occur to me. It is also inconsistent with the
other behavior of the dump reader.  For vectors, 1d arrays and row_vectors,
will read vectors in which there is no dimension attribute. That only
chokes in the case when the length of the vector/array is 1.

I share your annoyance this is all because R has no concept of scalars.  I
wonder if there is an alternative to using R dumps; maybe something like
protobuf.

This isn't about discouraging arrays of length 1. These instances arise
when the same model applies to cases with n>=1, the n isn't known until
run-time, and it wouldn't make sense to write a separate model for just the
n=1 case. For example, I have factor model code, in which there are several
vectors of length equal to the number of factors; when there is 1 factor
they have length 1. This issue arises often enough that I wrote my own dump
function to handle it
(https://github.com/jrnold/StanExtras/blob/master/R/write_stan.R).

On Thursday, February 7, 2013 11:55:57 AM UTC-5, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
> I did not work on those models before, but learned a bit.  And I can help with it.

So in Stan, if we can write down the analytical form of some distribution that is specified conditionally, it would be good to go.  Some simple model in Geo would be fine definitely, but not sure some complex one.

Now that we have the multivariate normal parameterized in terms of the precision, we are in a better position to replicate GeoBUGS models. The joint precision matrix often takes the form

A - rho * B

where A and B are constant matrices and the parameter rho is restricted to (0,1) or maybe (-1,1). There is often no alternative but to calculate the log determinant of that by brute force (QR decomposition or whatever) but the derivative of the log determinant with respect to rho can be worked out analytically, so we can do the calculations in doubles.

Users can do some of these models now in Stan code, but multiplying rho by B promotes to a parameterized matrix that is often large so the auto-diff will be a bottleneck.

Ben

messages.subject: Thinking out loud about missing data
messages.subject_clean: Thinking out loud about missing data
messages.body_plain:
I've been reading about so-called "k Nearest Neighbor Density Estimators". This short paper

http://scholar.google.com/scholar?cluster=16043802846384639781&hl=en&as_sdt=0,33

compares three of these things. Basically, they are scalar functions of a vector --- based on Euclidean distances to other rows --- that are not exactly proper density functions (because they integrate to infinity) but converge pointwise to a genuine density function as the number of observations increases. In particular, the function being pushed in the above paper converges to a gamma density. So, someone could potentially utilize this function if it were implemented in Stan and live with the fact that it is not quite a proper density or utilize a gamma density and live with the fact that it is not quite the right function. My gut says that it wouldn't matter much either way relative to the magnitude of the problem I am contemplating, which is that the datamatrix could have an arbitrary missingness pattern.

If all the variables were continuous but partially missing, then a full Bayesian approach would be pretty straightforward: Make parameters for the missing cells, put priors on them, index-fiddle to put these parameters into the right locations in the datamatrix, use something from that article as your "likelihood", let Stan run until convergence, and get a whole bunch of completed datamatrices to use in a subsequent analysis. Basically, it is just a joint multiple imputation algorithm with relaxed parametric assumptions.

Finding the k nearest neighbors is computationally difficult. But among rows that are fully observed, you only have to calculate the Euclidean distances once. And among rows that are incompletely observed, you can calculate a partial sum of squared differences once based on the columns where both rows are observed once and then you just have to tack on the remaining sum of squared differences for the columns where one or both rows are filled with parameters. And even still, we could do the whole thing in doubles to find the k nearest neighbors and then handle the derivatives manually. In other words, we don't need to mess with the derivatives for the (k + m)th distances because they never enter the "likelihood".

If the datamatrix includes discrete variables with missingness, we are not completely stuck by the fact that Stan can't do discrete parameters yet. Explode discrete variables into a full set of dummy variables and if missing, define an underlying parameter as a simplex of probabilities with some reasonable prior. The contribution to the total sum of squared differences for those columns is just 2.0 times the probability that the discrete variable differs between the two rows. To see this, say you have a variable like education with four levels (less than high school, HS or GED, some college, college degree). Then you might have two fully observed people that were both category two

row i: [...,0,1,0,0,...]
row j: [...,0,1,0,0,...]

in which case the contribution to the sum of squared differences is zero. Or two observed people with different levels of eduction

row i: [...,0,1,0,0,...]
row j: [...,0,0,0,1,...]

in which case the contribution to the sum of squared differences is 2. So, if row j were instead missing, the contribution to the sum of squares would be 2 times the probability that j is not in the HS / GED category. If both i and j were missing, then the contribution to the sum of squares is more complicated to calculate but has the same basic form. When Stan is done, you can draw realizations from a multinomial distribution with the corresponding posterior probability vector as your imputations.

Of course, that assumes it is reasonable to say that the "distance" between i and j is the same and has a weird cardinal value no matter how i and j differ in their education levels. E.g. if i drops out of high school and j graduates from college, they have the same distance as if i graduates from high school and j drops out of college. But at least the contribution to the distance is zero for two people with the same education level, and the fact that you have missing data on discrete variables is a much bigger problem.

I can't think of anything clever to deal with variables that are counts, but it is probably fine to treat them as continuous, impute missing elements with real parameters, and perhaps round the imputed values to the nearest integer once Stan is finished.

Thoughts?
Ben

master into your branch, too.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Friday, February 8, 2013 2:16:51 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> (Especially to Michael, Peter and Yuanjun:)
>
> I'm going to work on the following two issues:
>
>    master:  changing model/sampler data structures to Eigen
>             vectors
>
>    fvar branch: modify models to compute Hessians, gradient
>                 of trace of matrix-Hessian product, etc.,
>                 using forward-mode auto-dif
>
> I'd like to make sure I don't hose anyone else's work in
> the process.

In principal, it is impossible to lose data in git. You could create merge conflicts, but those are arguably a good problem (two people have made mutually exclusive changes to the same line) and easily resolved.

> Is it OK if I work on the updates in master, then merge
> master into fvar?  Yuanjun -- you'll have to merge the new
> master into your branch, too.

Someone should be merging master into remote branches at fairly regular intervals anyway. I don't think there is a technical problem with modifying master in anticipation of fvar being (re)merged eventually (as long as the code is not actually being called until fvar has been incorporated). But neither would there be a technical problem with modifying fvar and merging the whole thing into master whenever it is ready.

Ben

messages.subject: diag vs. nondiag models in bug examples.
messages.subject_clean: diag vs. nondiag models in bug examples.
messages.body_plain:
I compared the performance of three sampling schemes in fitting bug models,
1. default stan(diagonal matrix)
2. nondiagonal mass matrix shrinking to the diagonal part
3. nondiagonal mass matrix shrinking to both the diagonal and the identity matrix.

I choose to compare in terms of median time per n_eff since it tends to be stable comparatively. The result shows that nondiagonal sampling scheme generally performs better when dimension of the parameters are < 100. method 3(shrinking to identity) is a little better than method 2. However, for higher-dimensional paramters, the nondiagonal methods lose its power.

However, the result is noisy in that one stuck chain may lead to very poor mixing and n_eff. It is possible that randomness plays an important part in assessing the performance.

The result is attached.

Yuanjun

I have had some experiences of chains getting stuck - occasionaly the epsilon value became very small. The way I fixed this was to restart the epsilon calculation, using a new estimate of the initial epsilon, under certain conditions during burnin. For example, if alpha became very small and the number of depths hit the maximum.

The initial epsilon estimate can be far from good if the curvature at the starting point is very different to that at the minimum.

Of course, you can get stuck in a mode, but that is another story.

Saddle points can cause problems with sticking also.

At the end of the day, my approach is to use a variety of samplers (NUTS, DREAM, RWM) with different characteristics, so they can unstick each other.

ps I did a lot of work 9 months ago on non diagonal mass matrices with multivariate distributions, they did indeed give great performance in high dimensions with high correlations, I also used BFGS during burinin which also gave great results, but of course this is only applicable with fixed hessian, and you need other methods to handle the general case, as y'all know.

I'm fixing the test now. I'm going to look through Eigen's documentation for the spec. I'll let you know if I find any definitive answer.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
So, the real use case is to use what we just fixed:
stan::math::get_base1()

(the one with 4 params)

We were having difficulty assigning when we did something like (not compilable, but close):
-----
Matrix<double,Dynamic,Dynamic> x(2,3);
x << 1,2,3,4,5,6;
Matrix<double,1,Dynamic> y(1,3);
y << 101,102,103;

assign(get_base1(x,1,"x",1), y);
----

As you might imagine, assign() assigns the second argument to the first. Our original implementation had get_base1() returning a Matrix, but that resulted in a copy, so that assignment was no good. In order to fix that, we're now returning an Eigen::Block<MatrixType>, where MatrixType is the type of matrix we're using. Eigen::Block allows assignment, but that's the thing that doesn't have operator() defined for a single argument.

We tried to use .row(), but under the hood, that's a RowXpr. I couldn't figure out how to get the compiler to recognize that it would be assignable. This is deep in Eigen's expression templates.

So far, I've deduced that Eigen::Block is actually an Eigen::DenseCoeffsBase. I haven't figured out why that doesn't have an operator() with one argument.

Any insights?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Rstan: can I save a compiled model?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Rstan: can I save a compiled model?
messages.body_plain:
Hi--how about this example from that page:
---

fit1 <- stan(file = '8schools.stan', data = schools_dat,
             iter = 1000, chains = 4)
Once a model is fitted, we can use the fitted result as an input to fit the model with other data or settings. This would save us time of compiling the C++ code for the model. By specifying parameter fit for function stan, we can fit the model again. For example, if we want to sample more iterations, we can proceed as follows.

fit2 <- stan(fit = fit1, data = schools_dat, iter = 10000, chains = 4)
---

Yes, you do need data to compile the model that first time, but then when you re-run the compiled model you can feed in new data.  The data you use for compiling the model can be anything---actually, if we really wanted, we could create a "compile-only" mode for Stan where you would supply the model with no data, then Stan could just compile with fake data (e.g., setting all unconstrained parameters to 0, setting positive parameters to 1, setting constrained parameters to the midpoint of their range, etc) and then running for just 1 iteration to give it a chance to catch any gross bugs.  I don't know if that setting would be worth creating or not.  It's one more option (thus making life more complicated) but maybe it would be helpful.  But, in the meantime, you can certainly do this yourself by simply compiling the model and running for 10 iterations with whatever data you want.
AG

messages.body_plain:
I guess I am probably the biggest proponent of tightening the connection between Stan and Eigen, but I don't know that there is anything that absolutely has to go into v1.1.2. The main things are

-- With a std::vector it is ambiguous as to whether the thing is going to be used as a vector in the linear algebra sense or just as a holder for some scalars. So, you have to actually read the code to find out. With Eigen, you have a pretty clear separation between Eigen::Matrix (or Eigen::Vector) and Eigen::Array and can tell it a glance whether the function is doing linear algebra stuff.

-- There are more (relevant) coefficient-wise operations defined for Eigen objects than for std::vectors. This link has many of them

http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/AsciiQuickReference.txt

Most of the STL operations (sorting, etc.) are not that common in statistical applications.

-- There is some scope for speed improvements with doubles, where Eigen does packetwise and Stan has been doing elementwise, that would also involve less code and scope for stupid bugs. Also, with -DNDEBUG we can turn off range-checking for accessing Eigen objects via (), which as far as I know can't be done with STL.

-- If mixed type operations ever get supported in Eigen (or we figure out how to make them work generally in Stan), then it would be good to have as much of Stan as possible using Eigen's idioms.

Ben

With regards to the changes, where do they need to be? Bob and I were trying to refactor from the generated code down into all of our internals. Some comments below.

On Mon, Feb 18, 2013 at 2:28 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I guess I am probably the biggest proponent of tightening the connection between Stan and Eigen, but I don't know that there is anything that absolutely has to go into v1.1.2. The main things are
>
> -- With a std::vector it is ambiguous as to whether the thing is going to be used as a vector in the linear algebra sense or just as a holder for some scalars. So, you have to actually read the code to find out. With Eigen, you have a pretty clear separation between Eigen::Matrix (or Eigen::Vector) and Eigen::Array and can tell it a glance whether the function is doing linear algebra stuff.

If we switched to Eigen::Matrix, wouldn't it be just as ambiguous? I don't think we're going to be able to tell whether a user wants an Eigen::Matrix vs an Eigen::Array.

Some of the difficulty we were having were with the reference LHS types of functions as well as reference argument types.

Can you help by pointing out exactly where the changes from std::vector to Eigen::Matrix would be useful? Once again, we're looking at the whole system, and maybe you can help narrow the focus down to something reasonable.

> -- There are more (relevant) coefficient-wise operations defined for Eigen objects than for std::vectors. This link has many of them
>
> http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/AsciiQuickReference.txt
>
> Most of the STL operations (sorting, etc.) are not that common in statistical applications.

In our probability distributions, we're trying to vectorize anyway. As of right now, we can't really make use of the coefficient-wise operations. When implemented naively, you might be able to make use of Eigen functionality, but since we're trying to vectorize using templates to save us from writing thousands of versions of the same function, we're not really making use of it now. Of course, we could write our matrix views (these don't exist yet) to use Eigen underneath. It's just going to be a hassle exposing all the Eigen functionality through the views.

> -- There is some scope for speed improvements with doubles, where Eigen does packetwise and Stan has been doing elementwise, that would also involve less code and scope for stupid bugs. Also, with -DNDEBUG we can turn off range-checking for accessing Eigen objects via (), which as far as I know can't be done with STL.

Less code is good. Stupid bugs bad. But I don't think turning off range checks is a good idea. Users are already tripping on indexing out of bounds. We're trying to give them the best error messages possible -- but if Stan just kicks for no apparent reason, I think it'll be even harder to debug. Besides, we should be testing index bounds in our code and we do except for the multivariate distributions. So I'm not sure what efficiency is to really be gained by turning off range-checking. I could be convinced otherwise, but I just think is just info on what could be done and not a real benefit for using Eigen.

> -- If mixed type operations ever get supported in Eigen (or we figure out how to make them work generally in Stan), then it would be good to have as much of Stan as possible using Eigen's idioms.

Cool.

Ben, do you have any suggestions on learning how to use Eigen's expression templates? I'm reading through the documentation now, but it's pretty sparse. As an example, I want a function to return a reference to a row or column and be able to use that as a LHS in an expression. We found out that using the expression template for row or column doesn't allow for the return of that function to be used on the LHS because Eigen creates a temporary copy. So instead, we used Eigen::Block. Unfortunately, the issue there is that Eigen::Block is not an Eigen::Matrix. It shows up as being an Eigen::DenseBase, which doesn't define the operator() for a single size type. So although we can use it to do some of the manipulations, now the return type can't be used for reference operations as well as being passed into other methods expecting an Eigen::Matrix. Have any suggestions on how to deal with these sorts of issues? If you want to see where we're having this trouble, it's in assign() in stan/agrad/matrix.hpp (which depends on a few functions in both agrad/matrix and math/matrix). There are some tests in test/agrad/matrix_test.cpp for assign that flex the code in this way.

Perhaps if I really understood the expression templates, I'd be able to proceed a little quicker through the refactoring.

messages.body_plain:
I think there are two issues here -- the Stan language
itself and how it's implemented under the hood.  Let me
summarize some of the things I've said before.

Here's the typing lineup as I see it:

   Stan                 Implementation
   --------------------------------------------

   real x;              T;

   vector[K] x;         Matrix<T,Dynamic,1>
   row_vector[K] x;     Matrix<T,1,Dynamic>
   real x[K];           vector<T>

   matrix[J,K] x;       Matrix,T,Dynamic,Dynamic>
   real x[J,K];         vector<vector<T> >
   vector[K] x[J];      vector<Matrix<T,Dynamic,1> >
   row_vector[K] x[J];  vector<Matrix<T,1,Dynamic> >

   real x[I,J,K];       vector<vector<vector<T> > >
   vector[K] x[i,j];
   ...

I think the issue that confuses users is that there are
three ways to make a 1D object, four ways to make a 2D
object,  four ways to make a 3D object, and so on.

As is, linear algebra's only defined on the Eigen types.

We could simply forbid 2D arrays, getting rid of these two types:

   real x[K];
   real x[J,K];

But I'd rather not eliminate the distinction between the
various kinds of Eigen objects.  It follows the Eigen
implementation which specializes the class template of
Matrix for rows=1 (col vector) and columns=1 (row vector),
adding new operations.

Eigen itself also has an Array type, which could be used
to impelement both of the above types instead of
std::vector.

The big issue for me with the typing (and also for Eigen)
is that it allows us to tell what's going to happen with
operations like:

   (row_vector,vector):scalar

or

   (vector,row_vector):matrix

?

Changing the way all this works at this point would be
a pretty big undertaking.  I'm just trying to change the
basic underlying type for the models, but I think I may
just back everything out -- the issue is that the parameters
get touched by a whole lot of the code base.

As far as efficiency goes, I don't think it's going
to make a measurable difference changing from std::vector<T>
to Matrix<T,Dynamic,1>.  The big speed improvement comes
from vectorizing our auto-diff operations -- our time's all going
to computing gradients.  You can see this
in the recent probability functions and in the new
matrix ops.  The matrix ops will reduce to double-based ops
now.

Three things that will help with speed are:

   -- basic Cholesky factor type
   -- caching solutions for cov and corr matrices
   -- vectorizing the Jacobian determinants for all
      the transforms

I've been meaning to do the last two for a while now.

Moving to Eigen mixed types, even if we make it work, is
only a small part of the efficiency puzzle.  If we got that
working, then we'd still have to vectorize.  For that, we'd have
to vectorize in the right way to deal with the Eigen expression
templates, which is another enormous undrtkaing.  Wherever Eigen
uses a matrix of var (that is, for any vector or matrix
containing parameters or transformed params or local variables
in a model), it's very inefficient to use that representation
directly.  Some other basic data types for auto-dif might help,
but I've never been able to figure out how to make it work.

Whew -- didn't mean to go on that long.

- Bob

On Monday, February 18, 2013 11:43:07 AM UTC-5, Daniel Lee wrote:
> With regards to the changes, where do they need to be? Bob and I were trying to refactor from the generated code down into all of our internals. Some comments below.

I would say eventually the goal should be to have a consistent API that makes sense, but we've gotten by without one thus far, so it's not urgent for 1.1.2.

> On Mon, Feb 18, 2013 at 2:28 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > I guess I am probably the biggest proponent of tightening the connection between Stan and Eigen, but I don't know that there is anything that absolutely has to go into v1.1.2. The main things are
> >
> > -- With a std::vector it is ambiguous as to whether the thing is going to be used as a vector in the linear algebra sense or just as a holder for some scalars. So, you have to actually read the code to find out. With Eigen, you have a pretty clear separation between Eigen::Matrix (or Eigen::Vector) and Eigen::Array and can tell it a glance whether the function is doing linear algebra stuff.
>
> If we switched to Eigen::Matrix, wouldn't it be just as ambiguous? I don't think we're going to be able to tell whether a user wants an Eigen::Matrix vs an Eigen::Array.

Here, I was thinking that it is easier for developers to understand the C++ by looking at the function signatures that distinguish between Eigen::Array and Eigen::Matrix. I assume that most users wouldn't understand the difference even if it were possible to specify one or the other.

> Some of the difficulty we were having were with the reference LHS types of functions as well as reference argument types.
>
> Can you help by pointing out exactly where the changes from std::vector to Eigen::Matrix would be useful? Once again, we're looking at the whole system, and maybe you can help narrow the focus down to something reasonable.

I used some Eigen::Array stuff in transform.hpp, particularly .head() and .tail(). Maybe idioms like that would be useful elsewhere in the code. I would say that if you were going to do a partial transition, just do the double based stuff under src/stan/math/. That would get a little speed and be less complicated than messing with vars.

>
> > -- There are more (relevant) coefficient-wise operations defined for Eigen objects than for std::vectors. This link has many of them
> >
> > http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/AsciiQuickReference.txt
> >
> > Most of the STL operations (sorting, etc.) are not that common in statistical applications.
>
> In our probability distributions, we're trying to vectorize anyway. As of right now, we can't really make use of the coefficient-wise operations. When implemented naively, you might be able to make use of Eigen functionality, but since we're trying to vectorize using templates to save us from writing thousands of versions of the same function, we're not really making use of it now. Of course, we could write our matrix views (these don't exist yet) to use Eigen underneath. It's just going to be a hassle exposing all the Eigen functionality through the views.

When Eigen refers to vectorization, they usually mean compiler vectorization to do things packetwise instead of elementwise. This would help, but only for operations on doubles. When Stan users refer to vectorization, they usually mean using a function that accepts a vector (and loops internally) rather than forcing them to explicitly loop over all the elements of the vector. This is convenient for them but can actually be slower, e.g. if they call two or more such functions that internally loop over the same length, it might be better for them to do one explicit loop with multiple operations inside. Eigen partially avoids this situation with their expression templates, so that the compiler can write code that does multiple things with only one pass over the loop. And when Stan developers refer to vectorization, we usually mean doing something clever about the derivatives so we don't put a lot of auto-diff stuff on the heap and that could benefit somewhat from vectorization in the first sense.

>
> > -- There is some scope for speed improvements with doubles, where Eigen does packetwise and Stan has been doing elementwise, that would also involve less code and scope for stupid bugs. Also, with -DNDEBUG we can turn off range-checking for accessing Eigen objects via (), which as far as I know can't be done with STL.
>
> Less code is good. Stupid bugs bad. But I don't think turning off range checks is a good idea. Users are already tripping on indexing out of bounds. We're trying to give them the best error messages possible -- but if Stan just kicks for no apparent reason, I think it'll be even harder to debug. Besides, we should be testing index bounds in our code and we do except for the multivariate distributions. So I'm not sure what efficiency is to really be gained by turning off range-checking. I could be convinced otherwise, but I just think is just info on what could be done and not a real benefit for using Eigen.

Range checking should be on by default, but the user should ideally be able to turn it off once it is verified that the model is running properly.

>
> > -- If mixed type operations ever get supported in Eigen (or we figure out how to make them work generally in Stan), then it would be good to have as much of Stan as possible using Eigen's idioms.
>
> Cool.
>
> Ben, do you have any suggestions on learning how to use Eigen's expression templates? I'm reading through the documentation now, but it's pretty sparse. As an example, I want a function to return a reference to a row or column and be able to use that as a LHS in an expression. We found out that using the expression template for row or column doesn't allow for the return of that function to be used on the LHS because Eigen creates a temporary copy. So instead, we used Eigen::Block. Unfortunately, the issue there is that Eigen::Block is not an Eigen::Matrix. It shows up as being an Eigen::DenseBase, which doesn't define the operator() for a single size type. So although we can use it to do some of the manipulations, now the return type can't be used for reference operations as well as being passed into other methods expecting an Eigen::Matrix. Have any suggestions on how to deal with these sorts of issues? If you want to see where we're having this trouble, it's in assign() in stan/agrad/matrix.hpp (which depends on a few functions in both agrad/matrix and math/matrix). There are some tests in test/agrad/matrix_test.cpp for assign that flex the code in this way.

The most extensive thing is

http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/TopicInsideEigenExample.html

Ben

On 2/18/13 2:17 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:

> When Eigen refers to vectorization, they usually mean compiler vectorization to do things packetwise instead of
> elementwise. This would help, but only for operations on doubles. When Stan users refer to vectorization, they usually
> mean using a function that accepts a vector (and loops internally) rather than forcing them to explicitly loop over all
> the elements of the vector.

Right.

 > And when Stan developers refer to vectorization, we
 > usually mean doing something clever about the derivatives so we don't put a lot of auto-diff
 > stuff on the heap and that
 > could benefit somewhat from vectorization in the first sense.

Exactly.

 > This is convenient for them but can actually be slower, e.g. if they call two or more such
> functions that internally loop over the same length, it might be better for them to do one explicit loop with multiple
> operations inside.

It depends on the data layout.  The integer ops themselves
are relatively inexpensive and further, they can usually
be parallelized at the CPU level so that the time they add
to a bunch of double ops in the loop is zero.

If the data being looped over is local and you only do one
thing with it, then breaking it down into two loops can be faster.
If the data's not local and you do multiple things with it,
one loop can be faster.  If the data's not local and you do only
one thing with it, it probably doesn't matter.

> Eigen partially avoids this situation with their expression templates, so that the compiler can write
> code that does multiple things with only one pass over the loop.

Most of the expression templates are to avoid
copying/allocating data.  Doing multiple things in one
pass is a side effect.  So it's more efficient if you're
doing

     u = a * transpose(v) + w;

to not do the naive thing and allocate 3 new internal vectors
(1. transpose(v), 2. a * transpose(v), 3. a * transpose(v) + w)
and copy intermediate results into it, but to do the equivalent of:

   for (n in 1:N)
     u[n] = a * v[n] + w[n];

In some cases, Eigen will allocate intermediates to save
having to duplicate work, such as actually allocating a transpose
to do matrix multiplies so that you get better locality.
They use the traits to figure out when it's a win to allocate or not.

 >
>
>
>         -- There is some scope for speed improvements with doubles, where Eigen does packetwise and Stan has been doing
>         elementwise, that would also involve less code and scope for stupid bugs. Also, with -DNDEBUG we can turn off
>         range-checking for accessing Eigen objects via (), which as far as I know can't be done with STL.
>
>
>     Less code is good. Stupid bugs bad. But I don't think turning off range checks is a good idea. Users are already
>     tripping on indexing out of bounds. We're trying to give them the best error messages possible -- but if Stan just
>     kicks for no apparent reason, I think it'll be even harder to debug. Besides, we should be testing index bounds in
>     our code and we do except for the multivariate distributions. So I'm not sure what efficiency is to really be gained
>     by turning off range-checking. I could be convinced otherwise, but I just think is just info on what could be done
>     and not a real benefit for using Eigen.
>
>
> Range checking should be on by default, but the user should ideally be able to turn it off once it is verified that the
> model is running properly.

Agreed.    With the caveat that it's never possible to
tell if a model's running properly because you can do
something like:

     y ~ normal(0,1);   z <- x[round(y)];

and whether the index is in range or not depends on an
unbounded random quantity y.

For std::vector, the range-checking story is this:

    std::vector<double> x;

    double y = x[10];     // NO range checking

    double y = x.at <http://x.at>(10);  // YES range checking

We use x[10] throughout, so we just need to figure out how to

> > operations inside.

> are relatively inexpensive and further, they can usually
> be parallelized at the CPU level so that the time they add
> to a bunch of double ops in the loop is zero.

> thing with it, then breaking it down into two loops can be faster.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] GitHub Landing Page
messages.body_plain:
I've never used GitHub before Stan.

I'm thinking of GitHub as being nothing more than our
repository hosting.  As such, I want its readme to point
back to our home page and I want the rest of our GitHub
site to be totally minimal.

Maybe this isn't the right way to do it.  Maybe we should
just bail on maintaining our own home page and put
all our eggs in the GitHub basket.  If we can hack up one
landing page, we can probably add the dozen or so more we
have on our home page.

What I am absolutely opposed to is duplicating all of our
information across several sites.  I don't mind a few
high-level overviews, but I don't want the maintenance hassle
of writing the same detailed things that may change in multiple
places.

But please, let's not get too distracted by this issue.

- Bob

inline RealScalar squaredLength() const { return squaredNorm(); }

inline RealScalar length() const { return norm(); }

inline RealScalar invLength(void) const { return fast_inv_sqrt(squaredNorm()); }

template<typename OtherDerived>

inline Scalar squaredDistanceTo(const MatrixBase<OtherDerived>& other) const

{ return (derived() - other.derived()).squaredNorm(); }

template<typename OtherDerived>

inline RealScalar distanceTo(const MatrixBase<OtherDerived>& other) const

{ return internal::sqrt(derived().squaredDistanceTo(other)); }

inline void scaleTo(RealScalar l) { RealScalar vl = norm(); if (vl>1e-9) derived() *= (l/vl); }

inline Transpose<Derived> transposed() {return this->transpose();}

inline const Transpose<Derived> transposed() const {return this->transpose();}

inline uint minComponentId(void) const  { int i; this->minCoeff(&i); return i; }

inline uint maxComponentId(void) const  { int i; this->maxCoeff(&i); return i; }

template<typename OtherDerived>

void makeFloor(const MatrixBase<OtherDerived>& other) { derived() = derived().cwiseMin(other.derived()); }

template<typename OtherDerived>

void makeCeil(const MatrixBase<OtherDerived>& other) { derived() = derived().cwiseMax(other.derived()); }

const CwiseUnaryOp<internal::scalar_add_op<Scalar>, Derived>

operator+(const Scalar& scalar) const

{ return CwiseUnaryOp<internal::scalar_add_op<Scalar>, Derived>(derived(), internal::scalar_add_op<Scalar>(scalar)); }

friend const CwiseUnaryOp<internal::scalar_add_op<Scalar>, Derived>

operator+(const Scalar& scalar, const MatrixBase<Derived>& mat)

{ return
CwiseUnaryOp<internal::scalar_add_op<Scalar>,
Derived>(mat.derived(),
internal::scalar_add_op<Scalar>(scalar)); }

Then one can the following declaration in the config.h or whatever prerequisites header file of his project:

#define EIGEN_MATRIXBASE_PLUGIN "MatrixBaseAddons.h"

So, I think users could slip in arbitrary functionality.

messages.subject: Re: Thinking out loud about missing data and convergence
messages.subject_clean: Thinking out loud about missing data and convergence
messages.body_plain:
On Friday, February 8, 2013 2:38:50 AM UTC-5, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> I've been reading about so-called "k Nearest Neighbor Density Estimators". This short paper
>
> http://scholar.google.com/scholar?cluster=16043802846384639781&hl=en&as_sdt=0,33
>
> compares three of these things. Basically, they are scalar functions of a vector --- based on Euclidean distances to other rows --- that are not exactly proper density functions (because they integrate to infinity) but converge pointwise to a genuine density function as the number of observations increases.

Or ... is this potentially a convergence diagnostic (and a steak knife, etc.) My thinking here is that as the number of iterations increases a Markov chain converges to its stationary distribution and the non-parametric density estimator converges to the true density. Since we have the true log-posterior (ignoring normalizing constants) from Stan and can approximate the log-posterior non-parametrically, then the difference between them should become constant (i.e. zero if Stan didn't ignore normalizing constants).

This would at least make sense for a Gibbs sampler that moves every iteration. For a Markov chain with a Metropolis acceptance test, then sometimes the chain won't move from one iteration to the next. I presume one should exclude those when searching for the k-th nearest neighbors, but that may well affect the asymptotics and / or the optimal choice of k.

Here is an R function for the non-parametric density estimator pushed in the above paper:

kNN_DE <- function(x, k = floor(2 * nrow(x)^(1/ncol(x)))) {
  dist_x <- as.matrix(dist(x))
  dist_x[dist_x <= .Machine$double.eps] <- NA_real_
  N <- nrow(x)
  half_D <- ncol(x) / 2
  c_D <- pi^(half_D) / gamma(half_D + 1)
  P <- k / (N * c_D * apply(dist_x, 2, FUN = function(y) sort(y)[k])^ncol(x))
  return(P)
}

and a test with 8 schools

par(mfrow = c(2,1))
library(rstan)
fit <- stan_demo(model = "eight_schools", chains = 1, warmup = 0, iter = 4000,
                 seed = 123456, init = 0)

mat <- as.matrix(fit)
lp <- log(kNN_DE(mat[,-ncol(mat)]))
smoothScatter(1:nrow(mat), mat[,"lp__"] - lp, main = "Not Converged", las = 1,
              ylab = "Difference", xlab = "Post-warmup iteration")

fit <- stan_demo(model = "eight_schools", chains = 1, warmup = 1000, iter = 5000,
                 seed = 123456, init = 0)
mat <- as.matrix(fit)
lp <- log(kNN_DE(mat[,-ncol(mat)]))
smoothScatter(1:nrow(mat), mat[,"lp__"] - lp, main = "Converged", las = 1,
              ylab = "Difference", xlab = "Post-warmup iteration")

which yields

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-ovITzBIC1ts/USm6gGyVF9I/AAAAAAAAAHk/wtlST1pReLk/s1600/kNN_DE.png>
That at least looks pretty compelling. One limitation of non-parametric density estimators is that they do a worse job in the tails than near the mode, which may be what is happening at the iterations just before 3000.

Thoughts?
Ben
