messages.subject: abstracted autodiff on the road to RM-HMC
messages.subject_clean: abstracted autodiff on the road to RM-HMC
messages.body_plain:
I just pushed a reasonably complete agrad/autodiff.hpp
file to the fvar branch (fvar is where Peter Li and I
have been working on forward-mode auto-dif).

I implemented the design I sketched in the Stan meeting
last week, which lets users of C++ get at autodiff without
having to look at the autodiff types themselves.  The
basic rundown of operations is:

   single input, single output
   -- derivative                  (& function value)

   multiple input, single output
   -- partial derivative          (& function value)
   -- gradient                    (& function value)
   -- Hessian                     (& function val, gradient)
   -- gradient-vector dot product (& function val)
   -- Hessian times vector        (& function val)
   -- gradient of trace of matrix times Hessian

   multiple input, multiple output
   -- Jacobian                    (& function val)

Despite the seeming complexity, gradient-vector dot
product is just a directional derivative and can be done
using a single forward-mode autodiff pass.  The Hessian
times vector takes O(N) time, not O(N^2).  The graiden
of trace of matrix times Hessian takes O(N^2) time, not
O(N^3).

Here's an example of how they look from the C++ API:

     template <typename F>
     void
     hessian_times_vector(const F& f,
                          const Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& x,
                          const Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& v,
                          double& fx,
                          Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& Hv);

The typename F needs to be filled in with a functor that
defines an operator on Eigen vectors returning a scalar with the
type of the scalars and vector type templated out:

   struct fun1 {
     template <typename T>
     inline
     T operator()(const Eigen::Matrix<T,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& x) const {
       return x(0) * x(0) * x(1)
         + 3.0 * x(1) * x(1);
     }
   };

Then you can just define an instance of the functor:

   fun1 f;

and the arguments x and v,

   Matrix<double,Dynamic,1> x = ...;
   Matrix<double,Dynamic,1> v = ...;

and then set up locals to store the results into

   double fx;
   Matrix<double,Dynamic,1> Hv;

and then call the function

   hessian_times_vector(f,x,v,fx,Hv);

and now Hv now holds hessian times vector and fx the value.

So far, we can only define functions using underlying library
functions that are implemented for forward autodiff variables fvar.
But we'll work on getting this rounded out to all of the
Stan library functions.  (I'm hoping we can just further template out
the probability functions, which will only leave the matrix functions.)

- Bob

I think it would be zero asymptotically if Stan's lp__ reflected the normalizing constants. So, the difference will be non-zero but shouldn't be changing much as the number of draws from the stationary distribution increases.

> How do you monitor convergence of the density
> estimator?

I don't think anyone has derived great theoretical results. You can draw a finite number of times from a known joint distribution like multivariate normal and then see how long it takes for the non-parametric estimator to get close.

Ben

messages.subject: pairs function
messages.body_plain:
You can call pairs() on an object of class stanfit, but it tends not to look that good. So, I've written a custom one. It differs from pairs.default in the following ways

-- You can select which quantities to include via the pars argument (works the same way as in extract) which makes it more readable on smaller screens
-- You can select which chains to use via the chains argument
-- The diagonal has marginal histograms with all included chains
-- The labels on the diagonal parse as Greek
-- The default plot function for the off-diagonals is smoothScatter() rather than points(). This is a 2D kernel density plot of the intersection of the row-variable and column-variable.
-- The lower panel will plot the first "half" of the selected chains; the upper panel the rest. So if chains = 1:3, then the lower panel would include chain 1 only and the upper panel would pool chains 2 and 3. This is useful if you suspect one chain is out of whack and you want to compare it against a good chain.

Function attached. Plot inlined below. Complaints needed.

Ben

On Sunday, February 24, 2013 5:11:03 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I'd think in high dimensions, it'd be terrible, because
> no points are close to each other on average, so kNN tends
> to break down.

That is possible. The authors do recommend that k be a function of the dimensionality, namely 2 * N^(1/d). I did it with 10000 draws from a multivariate normal distribution with 24 highly correlated variables and it looked okay. I haven't been able to do it with a truly large number of dimensions yet because I haven't optimized the RAM enough to do much more than a 10000x10000 matrix of distances.

> At that point, what I see people in the
> machine learning literature do is try to find submanifolds
> of lower dimension on which the relevant values lie.

Possible. I don't know offhand how that would affect the convergence to the true density.

> But we're not really doing multivariate convergence analysis,
> just a bunch of marginals.  (I believe Brooks and Gelman extended
> R-hat to a multivariate setting.)

That is what I think is a problem with looking at convergence marginally. But I believe Gelman does not like the Brooks and Gelman statistic.

> Stan's lp__ should be OK up to a proportion -- I wonder how
> much of a problem we get by introducing an arbitrary rescaling?

I think it is not a problem at all, as long as you are just expecting the difference between the parametric and non-parametric to be a constant, rather than constantly zero.

messages.subject: the path-sampling diagnostic of convergence
messages.body_plain:
The challenge is that lp__ gives us the multivariate density, but density estimation works well in one dimension. One approach is to monitor one dimension at a time, integrating out all the others.  This can actually be done using path sampling.  Fan, Brooks, and I proposed such a convergence diagnostic in Section 5 of this paper:
http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/fanbrooksgelman.pdf
It was a cool idea but didn't seem so practical at the time.  With Stan, though, it could be done automatically, so maybe it is actually worth a try.
Andrew

On Feb 24, 2013, at 5:11 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> I'd think in high dimensions, it'd be terrible, because
> no points are close to each other on average, so kNN tends
> to break down.   At that point, what I see people in the
> machine learning literature do is try to find submanifolds
> of lower dimension on which the relevant values lie.
>
> But we're not really doing multivariate convergence analysis,
> just a bunch of marginals.  (I believe Brooks and Gelman extended

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] abstracted autodiff on the road to RM-HMC
messages.body_plain:
Awesome!

On Feb 24, 2013, at 3:35 AM, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> I just pushed a reasonably complete agrad/autodiff.hpp
> file to the fvar branch (fvar is where Peter Li and I
> have been working on forward-mode auto-dif).
>
> I implemented the design I sketched in the Stan meeting
> last week, which lets users of C++ get at autodiff without
> having to look at the autodiff types themselves.  The
> basic rundown of operations is:
>
>  single input, single output
>  -- derivative                  (& function value)
>
>  multiple input, single output
>  -- partial derivative          (& function value)
>  -- gradient                    (& function value)
>  -- Hessian                     (& function val, gradient)
>  -- gradient-vector dot product (& function val)
>  -- Hessian times vector        (& function val)
>  -- gradient of trace of matrix times Hessian
>
>  multiple input, multiple output
>  -- Jacobian                    (& function val)
>
> Despite the seeming complexity, gradient-vector dot
> product is just a directional derivative and can be done
> using a single forward-mode autodiff pass.  The Hessian
> times vector takes O(N) time, not O(N^2).  The graiden
> of trace of matrix times Hessian takes O(N^2) time, not
> O(N^3).
>
> Here's an example of how they look from the C++ API:
>
>    template <typename F>
>    void
>    hessian_times_vector(const F& f,
>                         const Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& x,
>                         const Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& v,
>                         double& fx,
>                         Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& Hv);
>
> The typename F needs to be filled in with a functor that
> defines an operator on Eigen vectors returning a scalar with the
> type of the scalars and vector type templated out:
>
>  struct fun1 {
>    template <typename T>
>    inline
>    T operator()(const Eigen::Matrix<T,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& x) const {
>      return x(0) * x(0) * x(1)
>        + 3.0 * x(1) * x(1);
>    }
>  };
>
> Then you can just define an instance of the functor:
>
>  fun1 f;
>
> and the arguments x and v,
>
>  Matrix<double,Dynamic,1> x = ...;
>  Matrix<double,Dynamic,1> v = ...;
>
> and then set up locals to store the results into
>
>  double fx;
>  Matrix<double,Dynamic,1> Hv;
>
> and then call the function
>
>  hessian_times_vector(f,x,v,fx,Hv);
>
> and now Hv now holds hessian times vector and fx the value.
>
> So far, we can only define functions using underlying library
> functions that are implemented for forward autodiff variables fvar.
> But we'll work on getting this rounded out to all of the
> Stan library functions.  (I'm hoping we can just further template out
> the probability functions, which will only leave the matrix functions.)
>
> - Bob
>

> --

> To unsubscribe from this group and stop receiving emails from it, send an email to stan-dev+u...@googlegroups.com.

messages.body_plain:
One problem is that we translate from unconstrained to constrained to
evaluate the log-density. This shows up with the gamma(0.01, 1) too,
whose left tail looks almost identical to the beta(0.01, 1)
distribution. If we have
x ~ gamma(0.01, 1)
then a typical draw for x is in the range of exp(-1000) to 5 or so.
But of course exp(-1000)=0 at double precision, and log(0) is outside
of the support of the unconstrained variable.

A workaround is to do something like this for the gamma(a, b):

parameters {
  real logx;
}
transformed parameters {
  real x;
  x <- exp(logx);
}
model {
  lp__ <- lp__ + a * logx - b * x;
}

or this for the beta(a, b):

parameters {
  real logitx;
}
transformed parameters {
  real x;
  x <- inv_logit(logitx);
}
model {
  lp__ <- lp__ - a * log(1 + exp(-logitx)) - b * log(1 + exp(logitx));
}

But that's not ideal. I'm not sure what we can do about this within
our current architecture, which really wants to transform beta r.v.s
to [0, 1] and gamma r.v.s to [0, inf].

Matt

I'll have to think about this for a bit longer.
It's a second-order directional derivative,

    tr(A*H) = SUM_n  A[n,n] * d^2/dx[n]^2 f(x)

but I'm not sure I can just do that the same way
as a first-order directional derivative (initialize
the second order derivative for x[n] to A[n,n] instead
of 1).  Let me get some paper out and get back to you.

What I've implemented so far is just what Michael needed
for RM-HMC, which is

    grad tr(M*H).

I could also pull out a more efficient O(N^2)
version of tr(M*H) alone that skips the last backward
pass (and thus has double types instead of agrad::var
reverse-mode types).

And when I'm writing O(N^2), it's really proportional
to O(N) function evals, where I'm assuming each of those
is O(N).  If the log probability function is more intense,
as when it contains nasty O(N^3) matrix ops, then it's
more complex.  I should write this some other way,
like O(N * f(N)), where f is the order of a log prob
function eval for inputs of size N.

- Bob

messages.subject: logit_beta
messages.body_plain:
We could pretty easily add a version of beta for logit-scaled parameters
directly,

   logit_beta(y|a,b) = beta(inv_logit(y)|a,b) * |d/du inv_logit(u)|_y,

which is arithmetically stable for y after a bit of algebra,

   log logit_beta(y|a,b) = alpha * log_sum_exp(0,y)
                         + beta * log_sum_exp(0,-y)
                         + lgamma(a + b) - lgamma(a) - lgamma(b).

But what should we do if a or b is close to 0?

We have a further issue when a and b in beta(a,b) are themselves
parameters, becuase what's really going on is beta(exp(a'),exp(b'))
where a' and b' the unconstrained parameters being sampled by HMC/NUTS.

If inv_logit(y) is used as a probability parameter in
bernoulli or binomial, we can deal with it directly using bernoulli_logit
and binomial_logit.  So an explicit beta binomial model would be

     logit_theta ~ logit_beta(a,b);
     n ~ binomial_logit(N,logit_theta);

where inv_logit(logit_theta) has the same distribution as theta under
the standard parameterization,

     theta ~ beta(a,b);
     n ~ binomial(N,y);

The logit version should be more efficient and more arithmetically
stable because we don't have to do any transforms of the parameters.

- Bob

messages.subject: isolating parameters for Gibbs sampling
messages.body_plain:
Warning:  the punchline's in the very last paragraph.

On 2/27/13 10:35 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> I was thinking of doing the hack where we Stan would alter the parameters-to-be-sliced
 > one at a time and examine which lines of the model change, thus it would build a
 > "hash table" (if I'm using that term correctly) telling it which lines of code
 > to compute for each part of the slice updating.

By "parameters to be sliced", Andrew's talking about
conditional sampling for unbounded discrete parameters (I now
am confused about whether to call this "Gibbs" given that
we don't have conjugacy relations so we don't sample the
conditional exactly).

This would be easy if for parameter theta[k], we could efficiently
evaluate the conditional

    log p(theta[k] | theta[1...k-1], theta[k+1,...K], y)

up to a constant that doesn't depend on theta[k].

It's the same issue for exact multinomial sampling
for bound parameters or if we wanted to do Gibbs
sampling of continuous variables for some reason.

It's easy to compute the above because it's proportional to
the joint posterior

    log p(theta | y )

which we already have up to a constant.  But that's very
very inefficient.

I understand what Andrew wants to do in principle.  (Yes,
it would be a hash table that maps from parameters to
sequences of lines of code.  Abstractly, a hash table
implements a function from one type of object to another.
A list in R implements such a map from names to values.)

But it's a whole lot harder to literally do what Andrew's
asking than it sounds.  If Stan were interpreted line-by-line
it would be more feasible.

For instance, consider this simple coding for regression:

    for (n in 1:N) {
       real mu;
       mu <- alpha + beta * x[n];
       y[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma);
    }

If alpha changes, we need to evaluate this whole thing.
Ditto beta.  But they only show up on the line with the
assignment to the local variable mu.

One angle we could use is our current propto calculations
which is what lets us compute the log joint efficiently up
to a constant.  If we could somehow make theta[k] the only
"variable" from the perspective of our trait metaprograms,
we'd pretty much get the behavior we wanted for free.

- Bob

I have checked in the code for exposing grad_log and grad_log_prob and the function for transforming parameters between its support and the unconstrained space to R.  The log_prob and grad_log_prob only takes parameter values on the unconstrained space.

An example of using them:

mcode <- '
  transformed data {
    vector[5] v;
    v[1] <- 1;
    v[2] <- 2;
    v[3] <- 3;
    v[4] <- 4;
    v[5] <- 5;
  }
  parameters {
    simplex[5] y;
  }
  model {
    y ~ dirichlet(v);
  }
'

library(rstan)
K <- 5
fit <- stan(model_code = mcode)
lp <- log_prob(fit, rep(0, K - 1))
gr <- grad_log_prob(fit, rep(0, K - 1))
y <- constrain_pars(fit, rep(0, K- 1))
uy <- transform_pars(fit, y)

Fix a typo in the manual regarding simplex transform:
https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/commit/845f62fcbc02f8d2c17af0bcb81d3797921b6274

Fix io/writer for unconstrain_simplex:
https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/commit/f718dc9d004580c34d8d33d5e050e565bf47a439

There is roundtrip test for simplex transformation for stan/prob/transform.hpp.  But the tests for io/writer does not include for the correctness of transformation.

Absolutely -- that's a positive for what we want to
do with it, which is run optimization code.

More below the example.

> An example of using them:
>
> mcode <- '
>    transformed data {
>      vector[5] v;
>      v[1] <- 1;
>      v[2] <- 2;

> library(rstan)
> K <- 5
> fit <- stan(model_code = mcode)
> lp <- log_prob(fit, rep(0, K - 1))
> gr <- grad_log_prob(fit, rep(0, K - 1))
> y <- constrain_pars(fit, rep(0, K- 1))
> uy <- transform_pars(fit, y)

This looks fantastic -- it's everything we need to
get going with it in R applications like optimization.

Some suggestions

1.  I think we need to add a method to the model that
lets us get the numbers of constrained and unconstrained
parameters.  That should simplify error checking in
the interface.  From the R side, it'd be something like

      K_unc <- num_params(fit)

We can't do this until we get in and modify the model to
return it.

2.  Can we give constrain_pars and transform_pars
complementary names?  I'm thinking

      theta <- constrain_pars(fit, theta_unc);

      theta_unc <- unconstrain_pars(fit, theta);

or

      theta_trans <- transform_params(fit, theta);

      theta <- inv_transform_params(fit, theta_trans);

I was rather inconsistent in our API and used "free"
in the transform code instead of "unconstrain".  Daniel and
I keep meaning to set aside some time to clean up the naming
throughout.

3.  I find the use of R constructs in examples confusing.
The R doc does it everywhere, but for us novices, simpler
is better.  So I'd suggest an example along the lines of

  theta_trans <- rep(0,K-1);  # unconstrained parameters

  theta <- inv_transform_pars(fit, theta_trans);

4.  The doc needs to point people to the transform doc so
they can figure out how many unconstrained parameters correspond
to their model.  But for the most part, if they work on the
constrained space as we have users do in Stan, the transforms will
all be under the hood.

5.  It'd be really great if we could read unconstrained
variables to transform out of an environment or list as inits
are handled now.  I think that'd make the R interface cleaner
from an R point of view.

messages.subject: random number generators in probs
messages.body_plain:
Peter:

I'd start with the univariate continuous distributions,
which live in:

   src/stan/prob/distributions/univariate/continuous

This work should be done on the main branch unless you'd
be more comfortable working on your own branch.  The reason
I suggest the main branch is that unlike the fvar stuff,
these being incomplete won't break the model compilation.

If you do want to keep working in fvar, you should merge
the master branch into fvar first so that you're reasonably
up to date with stan/prob.

There's currently a single example implementation in:

src/stan/prob/distributions/univariate/continuous/normal.hpp
------------------------------------------------------------
     template <class RNG>
     inline double
     normal_rng(double mu,
                double sigma,
                RNG& rng) {
       using boost::variate_generator;
       using boost::normal_distribution;
       using stan::math::value_of;
       variate_generator<RNG&, normal_distribution<> >
         rng_unit_norm(rng, normal_distribution<>());
       return mu + sigma * rng_unit_norm();
     }

where RNG is the templated out type of the basic random number
generator.  The use of a reference type ("RNG&") in the variate_generator
is critical in order to advance the shared random number generator we're
going to use.

This implementation samples from a Normal(0,1) distribution then
scales by multiplying by sigma (the scale parameter) and relocates
by adding mu (the location parameter).

Boost supplies many of the basic distributions and the Wikipedia
has pretty good descriptions of how to sample from the various
distribtuions.

I'm not sure how best to test these.  The current test is rather
weak, to say the least:

src/test/prob/distributions/univariate/continuous/normal_tes.cpp
----------------------------------------------------------------
TEST(ProbDistributionsNormal, random) {
   boost::random::mt19937 rng;
   EXPECT_NO_THROW(stan::prob::normal_rng(2.0,1.0,rng));
}

Anyone have any suggestions?  We could draw thousands of samples
and then make sure the sample-based estimates are within the
sampling variance at a very high threshold (so we don't create
a lot of false positive tests).  We can also do things like
test that the output is finite and appropriately signed (e.g.,
gamma variates should be positive, uniform variates shold be
constrained between their endpoints, etc.)

- Bob

On Thursday, February 28, 2013 5:34:22 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I'm not sure how best to test these.  The current test is rather
> weak, to say the least:
>
> src/test/prob/distributions/univariate/continuous/normal_tes.cpp
> ----------------------------------------------------------------
> TEST(ProbDistributionsNormal, random) {
>    boost::random::mt19937 rng;
>    EXPECT_NO_THROW(stan::prob::normal_rng(2.0,1.0,rng));
> }
>
> Anyone have any suggestions?

We could do a test of the null hypothesis that the pseudo-random values (with a given seed) came from the supposed distribution. A chi-square test

http://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda35f.htm

is probably the easiest to implement and using a more powerful test would just increase the chance of a false positive.

Ben
